newsitem.title: USA: Storms won't harm Carolina, Puerto Rico credit - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Storms won't harm Carolina, Puerto Rico credit - S&P.

text.p: Damage from hurricanes Fran and Hortense may strain some local budgets, especially in North Carolina, but should have no municipal credit impact in the southeastern United States or Puerto Rico, Standard & Poor's Corp said Monday.
Hurricane Fran caused $1.6 billion of damage, excluding flood damage and self-insured losses, in North Carolina, Virginia, Washington D.C., Maryland, West Virginia and Pennsylvania last month.
In all, 114 counties in five states were declared federal disaster areas, making them eligible for federal aid through the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
"Standard & Poor's is reviewing damage information as it becomes available but does not expect a material adverse rating impact on issuers affected by Hurricane Fran," the rating agency said.
North Carolina was hardest hit and has 41 counties that have been declared federal disaster areas, S&P said.

Raleigh officials expect that city's costs to clean up storm damage, secure property and restore public utlities will be $9 million to $10 million, even after receiving substantial assistance from state agencies, S&P said.

Though it expects ultimatley to be reimbursed for most of those expenses, the city is identifying areas in the fiscal 1997 budget where it can cut expenses in order to maintain a strong cash position, S&P said.
"Many of the local issuers in North Carolian began new fiscal years on July 1, 1996, and therefore have much budgetary flexibility in addressing hurricane-related costs," the rating agency said.
S&P said its credit quality concern would focus on the Wilmington, Southport and New Hanover County area.

"This area was hit hard by Hurricane Bertha in July 1996, suffering significant damage costs and revenue losses during prime tourism season. The additonal costs and more substandial damage following Hurricane Fran will surely strain local budgets, even though many issuers' financial reserves historically have been strong," S&P said.

In Virginia, Hurricane Fran caused more than $340 million of damage and 39 counties were declared federal disaster areas. Hardest hit issuers were the counties of Pace, Rockingham, Warren and Madison, none of which S&P rates.
"The credit quality of other municipal issuers in the state Standard & Poor's does rate, is not expected to be hurt," S&P said.
Hurricane Hortense struck Puerto Rico on Sept 10. Damage estimate exceeded $300 million and were still rising, however no major infrastructure damage was reported, S&P said.
Puerto Rico was also declared a federal disaster area and is eligible for FEMA aid.
While islandwide flooding left over 85 percent of the residents without power and 93 percent without water service, most of those services have been restored, S&P said.

Agricultural damage, particularly to coffee and plaintain crops, was estimated at $125 million, but the island's critical tourism and manufacturing facilities were spared. The peak tourismseason traditionally does not begin until November.

"Standard & Poor's is monitoring reports as they become available and does not expect hurricane damage to have a material impact on the credit quality of Puerto Rico or its agencies' $14.6 billion of outstanding bonds," the rating agency said.

S&P said it takes into account issuers' vulnerability to natural disasters when it initially rates an issue. Traditionally, the rating agency said, federal aid covers up to 75 percent of disaster-related costs, with the balance paid by state and local governments.
